# Correspondence with Brunner et al. (2017)

Brunner, Konietschke, Pauly & Puri (2017), *Journal of the Royal Statistical
Society B* **79**(5), 1463–1485, doi:10.1111/rssb.12222.

## What the paper does

**Power study, p. 1480.** Data are generated by \(X_{ik}\sim N(\mu_i,1)\),
\(i=1,\dots,4\), \(k=1,\dots,n\), with balanced sample sizes
\(n_i\equiv n\in\{15,20\}\). Two alternatives are considered:

| | alternative | name in the paper |
|---|---|---|
| (a) | \(\mu=(0,0,0,\delta)\) | one-point |
| (b) | \(\mu=(\delta/4,\delta/2,3\delta/4,\delta)\) | increasing trend |

with \(\delta=0,\,0.1,\dots,1.6\). Results are in Table 5, p. 1479. Every group
has variance 1 and every design is balanced.

**Type I study, Table 2, p. 1477.** Sample sizes \(n_1=(5,5,5,5)\) and
\(n_2=(10,20,30,40)\), with a constant \(m\in\{5,10,20,25\}\) added to every
component. Scaling vectors
\(\sigma\in\{(1,1,1,1),\;(1,\sqrt2,2,\sqrt5),\;(\sqrt5,2,\sqrt2,1)\}\), giving
the balanced/unbalanced and positive/negative pairing settings.

## What our grids do

**The gradient design is his alternative (b).** Our shift vector is
\((0,\,0.25,\,0.50,\,0.75)\); his at \(\delta=1\) is
\((0.25,\,0.50,\,0.75,\,1.00)\). The two differ by a constant 0.25 in every
group, which no location-invariant test can see. Computed with
`population_omega_sq()` in `omega_scaling_helpers.R`, \(\omega^2\) agrees to
eight decimals in all five designs:

| design | \(\omega^2\) ours | \(\omega^2\) his |
|---|---|---|
| balanced homoscedastic | 0.07246377 | 0.07246377 |
| unbalanced homoscedastic | 0.06264875 | 0.06264875 |
| balanced heteroscedastic | 0.03011463 | 0.03011463 |
| positive pairing | 0.02873331 | 0.02873331 |
| negative pairing | 0.02432827 | 0.02432827 |

**The one-point design at \(\delta=1\) is his alternative (a)**, verbatim:
\(\mu=(0,0,0,1)\).

## Where we go beyond the paper

1. **Heteroscedastic power.** He runs power only under \(N(\mu_i,1)\), so all
   groups have variance 1 and all designs are balanced. We cross the \(\sigma\)
   vectors of his Table 2 with the shifts of his power study. There is no
   heteroscedastic power simulation in the paper, so those cells are ours.

2. **How the sample size grows.** He adds a constant \(m\) to every group, so
   the group-size ratios drift from 1:2:3:4 toward 1:1:1:1 as the sample grows,
   confounding size with balance. We scale by \(\bar n\) with fixed
   multipliers, holding \(q_i=n_i/N\) exactly constant along the sweep.

3. **Input distributions.** He uses normal, double-exponential and log-normal.
   We use the five Fleishman panels, which include the normal case as panel 1.
